Causative & Permission Verbs

Quem manda aqui?

Who's in charge here?

Five ways to talk about control in English: forcing, persuading, permitting and authorizing. Same idea, five different grammars, five different relationships of power.

Why this lesson matters

Tal coisa te deixa louco. Tal pessoa te deixa nervoso. Em português, deixar faz dois trabalhos ao mesmo tempo: permissão e causa.

In English, they're two different verbs. Your instinct will often reach for LET, because that's what "deixar" means most of the time. But a feeling someone causes in you is MAKE, not LET. "It lets me crazy" doesn't exist. "It makes me crazy" does.

One more thing before we start

Every "someone" and "something" you'll see in this lesson is a placeholder. "Someone" is already an object, and in a real sentence you'll almost never say the word "someone" itself, you'll use an object pronoun instead.

I → me he → him she → her it → it we → us they → them

So "make someone happy" becomes, in real life, make her happy, make him furious, make it worse. Keep an eye out for this across all five cases.

Before we start
  • Does anyone at home ever make you do chores you don't feel like doing?
  • What do you let your partner or roommate get away with?
  • Is there anything your family allows during holidays that they don't allow the rest of the year?
  • What does your boss make you do that you'd rather skip?
  • Has a colleague ever gotten you to change your mind about something?
  • What does company policy allow you to do that surprises new employees?
  • What do you make your kids do every single day, no exceptions?
  • What do you let them do that your own parents never let you do?
  • Is there anything you allow only on weekends?
  • What did your parents make you do as a child that you hated?
  • Did anyone ever get you to try something you were scared of?
  • What were you never allowed to do until you turned eighteen?

01

Make (object) + adjective

MAKE + OBJECT + ADJECTIVE (or comparative)

Not an action. A feeling or a state that something causes, in a person or in a situation. The adjective can also level up into a comparative: "it makes things worse", not just "it makes things bad".

Force
Permission

Sunday afternoon at the Miller house. Nobody is really in charge, but everyone in that room is feeling something, and something outside of them is causing it.

1
make her focused
The homework makes her focused, but the drawing makes her happier.
2
make him relaxed
Video games after a long week make him relaxed.
3
make him hungry
Chopping vegetables next to the stove makes him hungry.
4
make him calm
The dog sleeping at his feet makes him calm.
Push it further: extreme adjectives

Extreme adjectives already mean "very ___", so they don't take "very" itself. Use absolutely, completely or utterly instead.

tired→
exhaustedexausto(a)
hungry→
starvingfaminto(a), morrendo de fome
angry→
furiousfurioso(a)
scared→
terrifiedapavorado(a)
happy→
thrilledradiante, muito animado(a)
surprised→
astonishedpasmo(a), estupefato(a)
interesting→
fascinatingfascinante
bad→
awfulpéssimo(a), horrível

Not "very furious". Absolutely furious.

Same feeling, another verb

The traffic makes me furious.

Something outside causes it.

I get furious when I'm stuck in traffic.

You change state yourself. No object, no person in the middle.

This GET means become. It's a different job from the GET in Case 03, which means persuade. Same word, two grammars, don't mix them up.

Real talk Sem verbo de ação depois do objeto, só adjetivo. E esse objeto não precisa ser gente: "it", "things", "the situation" entram no mesmo lugar. O adjetivo também pode virar comparativo, "makes it worse" é tão comum quanto "makes me happy".

Long meetings that go nowhere make me

A compliment from my boss makes me

02

Make someone do

MAKE + person + BASE VERB

An action, and no choice about it. Someone with authority forces it.

Force
Permission

Gate 12. The line moves, the officer points, and nobody argues. This is what obligation looks like when it has a uniform.

1
make her take off her shoes
Security makes every passenger take off their shoes before the scanner.
2
make passengers empty their pockets
The machine makes travelers empty their pockets first.
3
make him show his passport
The agent makes him show his passport before printing the boarding pass.
Tap the pins, then borrow theseNumbered in the photo, then borrow these
make someone wait
make someone remove
make someone sign
make someone repeat
make someone show ID
Real talk Sem "to": "make her take off", nunca "make her to take off". Igual ao LET. O difícil aqui não é a gramática, é lembrar que não tem escolha.
Complete the one that fits your life

My manager always makes me before I leave the office.

Airport security makes every passenger before boarding.

My landlord makes tenants before moving out.

03

Get someone to do

GET + person + TO + VERB

Persuasion. There is a choice, but you work to influence it.

Force
Permission

The customer wasn't planning to spend that much today. Twenty minutes later, he's nodding at the estimate. Nobody forced him. Somebody just explained it well.

1
get him to approve the repair
The mechanic gets him to approve the repair by explaining exactly what's broken.
2
get him to sign the estimate
The receptionist gets him to sign the estimate before the work starts.
3
get him to trust the shop
Years of honest work get customers to trust the shop.
Tap the pins, then borrow theseNumbered in the photo, then borrow these
get someone to agree
get someone to understand
get someone to reconsider
get someone to calm down
get someone to commit
Real talk GET traz o "to" de volta, e muda o sentido: alguém foi convencido, não obrigado. "I got him to do it" soa bem mais diplomático que "I made him do it".
Complete the one that fits your life

It took me a week, but I finally got my landlord to the leak.

She got her coworkers to the new software without complaining.

I got the mechanic to me a better price.

04

Let someone do

LET + person + BASE VERB

Permission, informal. You don't stop it. You simply say yes.

Force
Permission

Saturday, the park is full, and for once nobody is in a hurry. Today the answer to almost everything is yes.

1
let her swing higher
Her mother lets her swing higher every time she asks.
2
let them go down the slide
The teacher lets them go down the slide two at a time.
3
let her build a sandcastle
Her dad lets her build a sandcastle as tall as she wants.
4
let her buy an ice cream
Her mom finally lets her buy an ice cream from the cart.
Tap the pins, then borrow theseNumbered in the photo, then borrow these
let someone choose
let someone stay
let someone go first
let someone try
let someone decide
Real talk Mesma estrutura de MAKE, sem "to", mas sentido oposto: um força, o outro permite. "Let her go" e "make her go" mudam a história inteira.
Complete the one that fits your life

My boss lets us from home on Fridays.

On weekends, I let myself until midnight.

Our neighbors let us their pool whenever we want.

05

Allow someone to do

ALLOW + person + TO + VERB

Permission, but official. A rule, a policy, an institution decides.

Force
Permission

Oakwood C.I. has a sign for everything. One rule says no. Right next to it, a glass box says yes, quietly, on its own terms.

1
doesn't allow students to use phones
The school doesn't allow students to use their phones during exams.
2
allows students to make private calls
The phone pod allows students to make private calls between classes.
3
allow her to leave early
The coordinator allows her to leave early on Fridays for her internship.
Tap the pins, then borrow theseNumbered in the photo, then borrow these
allow someone to enter
allow someone to bring
not allow someone to use
allow someone to submit late
allow someone to reschedule
Real talk ALLOW é o LET de terno: mesma permissão, mas com "to" e peso institucional. "My mom lets me" é natural. "My mom allows me to" soa quase um contrato.
Complete the one that fits your life

Company policy allows employees to two days a week from home.

The gym doesn't allow members to after 10 pm.

My contract allows me to once a year.

Same idea, five grammars

Before the quiz, look at all five side by side. This is the map you'll use every time you're not sure which one fits.

StructurePatternWho decidesFeel
Make + adj make + person + adjective the situation, not a person causes a feeling
Make + do make + person + base verb the one with authority no choice, obligation
Get + to do get + person + to + verb shared, through persuasion convinced, not forced
Let + do let + person + base verb the one who allows informal permission
Allow + to do allow + person + to + verb a rule or institution formal permission

Quick check

1. The dentist always _______ me nervous, even before he says a word.

2. It took the whole meeting, but she finally _______ the team to accept the new schedule.

3. Airport rules don't _______ passengers to carry liquids over 100ml.

4. My grandma always _______ us stay up late during the holidays.

5. The smell of fresh bread from the kitchen _______ everyone hungry.

Tap each numbered pin on the photo, then choose MAKE, GET, LET or ALLOW below.Each numbered scene below matches a number on the photo. Choose MAKE, GET, LET or ALLOW for each.

The line at the cashier is long. Nobody skips it. The store _______ every customer wait their turn.

Obligation, no choice, no "to". Makes is the one.

The boy in the cape wasn't sure about the Spider-Man toy. His dad _______ him to see how cool the box looked, and now he won't put it down.

Gentle persuasion, with "to". Got is the one.

The LEGO table is free to use for anyone. The store _______ kids build whatever they want there, no purchase required.

Informal, casual permission, no "to". Lets is the one.

The girl trying on the jester hat looks thrilled. Trying on hats before buying _______ her excited about the costume section.

A feeling, not an action, so it's followed by an adjective. Makes is the one.

Store policy _______ children to test any toy on the shelf before their parents pay for it.

A written rule, formal, with "to". Allows is the one.
